questions.question: Define a natural material, name five examples, and state one useful property and one limitation of each.
questions.expected_answer: A natural material is taken from plants, animals or the earth and used with little change. Timber: strong and easy to work, but rots, burns and warps. Clay: cheap and keeps water cool, but heavy and shatters. Leather: tough and flexible, but cracks when dry and rots when wet. Cotton: comfortable and absorbent, but holds water and dries slowly. Thatch: cool and local, but leaks and burns. (Also natural rubber: elastic but sticky in heat; stone: durable but heavy.) Natural materials also vary from piece to piece and are limited in supply.

questions.question: Distinguish between new materials and improved materials, giving two examples of each and the natural material each replaced.
questions.expected_answer: New materials are made by chemical or industrial processes and did not exist in nature: polythene (replaced clay and metal in buckets and tanks), PVC (replaced iron and clay pipes), nylon and polyester (replaced cotton, sisal and silk in ropes and clothing), polystyrene (replaced straw in packaging). Improved materials are natural materials treated or combined to overcome their limits: steel and stainless steel (improved iron, replaced timber beams and enamel pots), concrete (improved cement and stone, replaced cut stone and brick), plywood (crossed wood layers, replaced solid planks that warp), treated timber, glass fibre composites.

questions.question: Explain how the replacement of natural materials had a positive impact, listing the main kinds of benefit with an example of each, and state why the term also studies the negative side.
questions.expected_answer: Benefits: lighter (polythene bucket versus clay pot), stronger and more durable (steel beam versus timber), cheaper (mass-produced items more people can afford), safer (polycarbonate helmets, single-use plastic syringes), more consistent (identical factory materials make reliable products), more available (not limited by harvest or season). Examples of impact: PVC pipes and polythene tanks brought clean piped water to villages; concrete and steel housed millions; packaging keeps food fresh. The term also studies the costs, such as plastic waste, pollution and use of non-renewable oil, because a technologist must weigh benefits against harm and design to reduce it.
